title: Case 884: the carton serial did not match
public_context: Service businesses often separate a customer's request from the decision to refund, repair, or replace an item. Return records can combine serial checks, delegated approval limits, inspection results, and customer communication. Such records describe a particular case rather than a general warranty promise.
source_title: Pine Relay service desk return-authorization correspondence
source_text:
Case 884 arrived at the Pine Relay service desk with a request to exchange a countertop mixer for the same model. The customer had bought it from a regional dealer eleven days earlier and said it had stopped during kneading. The front desk clerk checked the receipt and found that the mixer body serial ended in 1842, while the carton label ended in 1482. The clerk did not issue a replacement token while the two identifiers disagreed.

The service manual allowed front desk staff to issue a refund below eighty credits only for an unopened item with matching serial labels. Opened equipment needed a bench note, and any safety-related fault required a supervisor to approve the remedy. The customer had opened the carton, so the request went to the bench. The technician found a split strain-relief sleeve on the power cord but no motor fault during the short no-load check. The sleeve was kept with the case tag for inspection.

A supervisor compared the body serial with the dealer invoice and confirmed that the body, not the carton, matched the purchase. The desk corrected the carton record and authorized a refund rather than an exchange because the damaged sleeve could not be returned to sale stock. The customer accepted the refund by phone that afternoon. No replacement mixer was shipped, and the original mixer remained in the safety-hold cabinet.

The clerk completed the return authorization with separate fields for serial correction, bench finding, and remedy. The service desk credited the dealer's account after receiving the returned unit, while the customer receipt showed the refund date and case number. The dealer signed the collection slip for the unit but left the optional comments field blank. The supervisor scheduled a cord inspection for the next safety review because two other mixers from the same delivery had similar sleeves.

The correspondence confirms that the refund was processed and the returned mixer stayed under hold. The desk closed the customer case but kept the safety review open under a separate tracking number. The clerk filed the dealer's signed collection slip behind the return authorization and carried the inspection tag into the review folder.
